readerTitle: The promo that worked too well
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 서비스, 소프트웨어 회사 영업팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 할인의 효과는 할인한 달이 아니라 그다음 몇 달에 나타난다. 고객이 '기다리면 싸진다'를 배우는 순간 할인은 스스로를 키우는 고리가 된다.
misconception: 할인 뒤 매출이 떨어지면 수요가 약해진 것이니 다시 할인하면 된다.

sources.text: 시스템 사고의 표준 개념 (강화 피드백 루프, 지연)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 청소 서비스와 소프트웨어 영업팀 사례는 모두 가상입니다. '평소 5월보다 약 3분의 1 감소', '25% 할인' 등 수치는 설명용이며 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
분기 말 할인이 B2B 소프트웨어 영업에서 흔하다는 서술은 일반적 관찰로만 썼고 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 특정 기업이나 통계를 덧붙이지 마세요.
피드백 루프(THK-06-01), 지연(THK-06-02) 개념 레슨의 용어 정의와 이 레슨의 표현이 일치하는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: The promo that worked too well
body: A home-cleaning company offers 25% off every booking in April. The phone rings all month. The calendar fills up.
In May, bookings fall below a normal May. So in June, the owner runs another promo. It works again. July is quiet again.

image.label: A cleaning calendar full in one month and empty the next
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 벽에 걸린 달력 두 장. 'April' 달력은 예약 스티커로 빽빽하고, 'May' 달력은 거의 비어 있음. 옆에 청소 도구 바구니와 '25% OFF' 전단지. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: May is slow. What now?
body: You own the cleaning company. April's 25% off deal filled the calendar. May bookings are down about a third compared with a usual May.
Your best cleaner asks if there will be enough hours next month. What do you do?

options.text: Run another 25% off deal in June to fill the gap
options.feedback: It fills June, but it feeds a **feedback loop**: each deal teaches customers to wait for the next one, which makes the next slump deeper.

options.text: Hold full price and check who booked in April before deciding
options.feedback: You accept a slow month to learn the cause. Because of the **delay** between a discount and its cost, May may be the bill for April, not a sign of weak demand.

options.text: Cut your regular price by 10% for good
options.feedback: It stops the stop-start pattern, but you lose margin on every job forever, based on one month of data that the promo itself distorted.

cards.title: Follow the calendar.
body: Nothing about the customers' homes changed. What changed was what customers learned about your prices.

breakdown.label: Promo month
breakdown.detail: Regulars book early to get the deal

breakdown.label: Second promo
breakdown.detail: The slump looks like weak demand

breakdown.label: New normal
breakdown.detail: Many customers book only on deals

cards.title: The discount feeds itself.
body: A **reinforcing feedback loop** is a chain where each step pushes the next one harder in the same direction.

Here it runs like this: a deal brings a spike. Customers learn that deals come back. They wait. Full-price bookings drop. The owner sees the drop and runs another deal. Each turn of the loop makes customers wait a little longer.

image.label: A loop diagram: discount, spike, waiting, slump, discount
image.brief: 원형 화살표 다이어그램. 'Discount' → 'Bookings spike' → 'Customers learn to wait' → 'Full-price slump' → 다시 'Discount'. 화살표가 돌수록 점점 굵어져 루프가 강해지는 느낌.

cards.title: The cost arrives after the credit.
body: The good news from a discount shows up the same week. The bad news shows up a month or two later, after customers have changed their habits.

That **delay** hides the link between cause and effect. By the time the slump appears, April feels like a success story. May looks like a separate problem, so the owner reaches for the tool that worked last time.
The fix is to judge a promo over the full cycle: the deal month plus the months after it.

cards.title: Now it's a sales team.
body: You lead sales at a software company that sells yearly subscriptions. For a few quarters, reps have offered extra discounts in the last week of each quarter to hit targets.
Now big customers stall all quarter, then call in the final week asking for the deal. What do you change?

options.text: Raise the quarter-end bonus so reps close even harder
options.feedback: More pressure in the final week means bigger discounts, which teaches customers to wait even longer. You speed up the **feedback loop** instead of breaking it.

options.text: Allow discounts only in exchange for something, like a longer contract or upfront payment, at any time of the quarter
options.feedback: Waiting stops paying off, so the loop loses its fuel. Expect a rough quarter or two first: the **delay** means customers take time to unlearn the habit.

options.text: Keep quarter-end discounts but cap them at 10%
options.feedback: Smaller discounts slow the damage, but the timing still rewards customers who wait. The loop runs, just more slowly.

cards.title: Not every discount starts a spiral.
body: The loop needs customers who can wait and who can predict the next deal. A plumber fixing a burst pipe can't be waited out. A deal tied to a clear reason, like first-time customers or off-peak hours, teaches less.
Also check what the slump really is. Some of it may be demand pulled forward: people who booked early and will return on schedule. That fades by itself. Learned waiting doesn't.

cards.title: Judge a discount by the months after it.
body: Two ideas did the work here. **Feedback loops:** each deal teaches customers to wait, which invites the next deal. **Delays:** the cost arrives weeks later, so it looks like a new problem.
**Try it today:** pick your last promotion. Compare sales for the two months after it with the same months a year earlier. Did customers come back at full price?
